items.title: RT Satya Sontanam: Recently sat with @deepakshenoy and @CalmInvestor to understand Capitalmind Mutual Fund’s Quant style of investing. When we think ...
items.description_html:
RT Satya Sontanam
Recently sat with @deepakshenoy and @CalmInvestor to understand Capitalmind Mutual Fund’s Quant style of investing.

When we think of an actively managed quant fund, it is less about actively picking stocks and more about actively managing the strategy.

Within quant, 'momentum' is at the core of their strategy, something Capitalmind has already been following through their PMS strategies.

But momentum has its weak periods too. When markets correct, it is uncomfortable to sit through the strategy.

So while the mutual fund strategy continues to focus on momentum, they want to prefer stocks with lower volatility, too — stocks that have moved more steadily rather than swinging sharply up and down.

As with every Know Your Fund Manager episode, we also discussed when this strategy is likely to do well and when it may struggle.

More here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=P6zVhuuPMtg

It was lovely finally meeting you both in person after following many of your tweets over the years. Thanks for doing this, Deepak and Anoop. Best wishes!

items.description_html:
Bector Foods delivered its best quarter in over a year and the FY27 setup only gets stronger from here.

OPM expanded to 13.1%, the highest print since Jun 2024, marking the fourth straight quarter of sequential margin improvement.

B2B bakery frozen is now roughly 20% of the segment, built over the last 2-3 years specifically around institutional and QSR demand. QSR consumption in India had been soft through FY26 but this qtr we have seen improvement in QSR in Q1.

If the broader QSR recovery holds through FY27, Bector's frozen and B2B bakery arm is one of the cleaner second-order beneficiaries

Capacity is built. Margin is compounding. And now the demand backdrop is starting to cooperate too.

📌 A new study has painted a worrying climate picture of Maharashtra.

📌The researchers studied Compound Drought and Heatwave (CDHW) events—where bone-dry conditions and scorching temperatures collide—from the state’s formation in 1960 till 2025.

📌1990 served as an inflection point for such events.

📌Rising temperatures can now trigger and amplify droughts even during the monsoon in the state.

📌As the Arabian Sea warms, Maharashtra’s wetter west—districts such as Nashik, Thane and Raigad—are emerging as hotspots.

🖊️ @himanshujourno

items.title: RT Kshitij Anand: After nerding out on 1991 reforms, I found out more things today that I was not aware of: - Chandrashekhar was PM when BOP crisis ca...
items.description_html:
RT Kshitij Anand
After nerding out on 1991 reforms, I found out more things today that I was not aware of:

- Chandrashekhar was PM when BOP crisis came into light and his government initiated IMF Loan sanction process which eventually led to us using our gold as collateral for the loan.

-New Economic Reform that Mr Singh brought to us was apparently heavily inspired by Yashvant Singh’s mini reform which he planned to present in early months of 1991 but couldn’t because he was a part of minority government and couldn’t convince allies and opposition.

PVN and Mr Singh was able to end to Licence raj and bring new reforms but that was not the first attempt to do that.

Government before them had the same intention but no political backing.

We hail MMS and PVN for bringing us out of a dark crisis but there were heroes in shadows who tried doing the same but couldn’t.

Credit should go where it’s due imo.

I was today’s year old when I knew what previous government did for BOP crisis that propped up under their regime.

For centuries, the Striped Hyena has been a mysterious creature across most of the Indian Subcontinent. The object of countless myths, the species has consequently received bad press and negativity.

A study conducted in the Purulia district of West Bengal’s Rarh region has focussed on this enigmatic animal. It shows that living near wildlife does not guarantee knowing them.

Researchers Vasudha Mishra, @tesstwit, Sayan Banerjee and @arjun_srivathsa found confusion over its identity, mixed feelings about its scavenging and stress the need for tailored, informative conservation outreach.

items.title: The Mother Who Wanted to Be Overtaken 🙏 There is something fitting about writing this while reading Dr Anji Reddy’s words. A man who built an inst...
items.description_html:
The Mother Who Wanted to Be Overtaken 🙏

There is something fitting about writing this while reading Dr Anji Reddy’s words. A man who built an institution of enormous scale still called his life’s work unfinished. Perhaps that is the real legacy.

Every balance sheet is a photograph. It tells you what a company looks like at a point in time, but not everything that is moving beneath it. The visible company is only the surface. The deeper asset is the ecosystem it helps create.

Divis overtook Dr Reddy’s in market cap some time ago. Laurus has now moved ahead of Dr Reddy’s as well. But I look at Dr Reddy's differently.

To me, Dr Reddy’s is like that mother who always wanted her children to shine and grow, even if one day they became bigger than her.

That is why it would be too naive to judge Dr Reddy’s, or the erstwhile Ranbaxy, purely by sales, margins and cash flows. Their contribution goes far beyond what appears in an annual report. They created scientists, entrepreneurs, manufacturing capabilities, regulatory knowledge, supplier networks, customer relationships and, perhaps most importantly, confidence.

They proved something that was once far from obvious. Indian science did not have to remain a technology beseecher. India could become a technology provider to the world.

Once that belief was proven, it became transferable. Scientists moved. People left and built new companies. Suppliers became stronger. Customers developed trust in Indian capabilities. Knowledge spread from one organisation to another. One company's achievement became another company's starting point.

That is how ecosystems compound.

A forest is not measured only by its tallest tree. The real strength lies in the soil beneath it.

Look at Indian pharma today. The number of companies building complex capabilities, developing new technologies and serving global customers is extraordinary. Many of them could not have existed in their current form without the pioneers who came before them.

This is what I think of when I read Dr Anji Reddy calling his life's work an unfinished agenda.

An unfinished agenda is not a failure to complete something. It is a refusal to believe that the work is ever complete.

Affordable medicine for the world was never a destination. Every disease that remains unsolved creates another frontier. Every new technology creates another possibility. Every generation has another boundary to push.

So let Dr Reddy’s be overtaken. Let Zydus be challenged. Let Divis grow. Let Laurus grow. Let the next generation build companies that make today's giants look small.

That would not diminish the legacy. It would prove that the legacy is alive.

The true measure of Dr Anji Reddy’s contribution is not whether the company he built remains number one forever. It is whether the ecosystem he helped create continues to produce people and companies capable of becoming number one.

That is the beautiful thing about an unfinished agenda.

The agenda must never finish. The end must never come.

Perhaps the greatest contribution of one generation is not reaching the destination. It is leaving behind enough capability, confidence and curiosity for the next generation to start from a much higher point.

We enjoy the journey more than the destination. And perhaps that is exactly how a great ecosystem keeps compounding.

items.title: Electronics Mart - Exceptionally strong quarter REV at 2,419 Cr (+39% YoY) EBITDA at 239 Cr (+118%) PAT at 121 Cr (+458%) EBITDA margin expanded sharp...
items.description_html:
Electronics Mart - Exceptionally strong quarter

REV at 2,419 Cr (+39% YoY)
EBITDA at 239 Cr (+118%)
PAT at 121 Cr (+458%)

EBITDA margin expanded sharply to 9.9% from 6.3%

SSSG was exceptionally strong at 34.2%, driven by healthy demand, higher footfalls, strong AC season & improving productivity of recently opened stores

South remains the core profit engine with REV growth of 40% & EBITDA margin of 10.9%. Andhra Pradesh grew 62% with 49% SSSG, while Telangana grew 48% with 40% SSSG

North also appears to have turned the corner - REV grew 29% & EBITDA margin improved to 4.9%. Management expects margins to gradually move towards South levels as stores mature

Store maturation is the biggest embedded margin lever. 96 mature stores delivered 11.2% EBITDA margin, while 131 stores less than 4 years old already reached 8.1%, materially ahead of earlier expectations

Management guided for FY27 REV growth of 18-20%. Despite the exceptionally strong Q1, management remains conservative given seasonality in cooling products

Gross margin expanded to 17.2% from 14.6%, aided by higher cooling product mix & temporary inventory gains from price increases in mobiles/laptops

Post Ind AS EBITDA margin guidance for FY27 is around 7.5-8%, versus historical levels closer to 6-7%, reflecting structural operating leverage from store maturation

Working capital improved materially with days reducing to 42 from 73 in March

West Bengal is the next major growth market. 5 stores are targeted by Diwali & 10-12 by FY27 end, with around 30 stores planned over the next 2 years

Management expects West Bengal stores to achieve faster payback than North. Existing South stores generally achieve payback within 10-11 months versus around 16-18 months in North

Market share gains are becoming visible, particularly in smaller South markets where management indicated gains ranging from around 4-12%, supported by the shift from unorganised to organised retail

Premiumisation remains another structural advantage. EMIL has historically focused on premium categories, allowing it to benefit disproportionately from higher demand for premium ACs, large TVs, refrigerators and other appliances

items.description_html:
Why #UPI transactions should be charged? Of course, at a nominal rate & only for certain transactions.
Now govt compensates banks, payment system operators & app providers through an incentive scheme for processing zero-MDR transactions. This scheme covers only 11% of actual industry costs.
Allocations under the incentive scheme coming down every year : Rs 1,500 cr in FY22, Rs 2,600 cr in FY23, Rs 3,500 cr in FY24, Rs 1,500 cr in FY25.
A system where Govt uses public money to subsidise one-seventh of market-rate costs is not an ideal pricing strategy.
Zero-MDR policy was introduced in January 2020 as a temporary measure to accelerate adoption. Subsidy in early phase fine. No-cost transactions played a key role in onboarding at least 500 mn users and millions of small merchants within a few years.
Adoption of digital payments remains concentrated in urban areas. Rural & underserved geographies lag on merchant acceptance infrastructure, connectivity & onboarding support.
A time-bound, tiered MDR on large commercial UPI merchants, with small merchants & individuals permanently exempted, is in order, & so is revenue allocated for strengthening infrastructure & rural expansion. @UPI_NPCI @DFS_India

Aerospace , Pharma , Metals , Chemicals lot of these sectors require global customer mapping , for us to realize the true depth of capability , competitive environment, profit pool mapping and where they stand, we need to know what is the situation at the customer end

The type of customers will make it easy to determine the growth you will see here , if in a pharma company the customer is top 10 pharma with heavy skew in phase 3 molecules in a particular therapy such as ADC/peptides then you map out who in the world has done the capex in that in India , most of them you cant find directly on relationships as they have NDA's but you will easily get a broad idea , and then map out the commercial performance of that molecule to see if the Indian player is a preferred supplier or in a category of suppliers , then you can quantify the kind of growth Metals + Chemicals = China , the giant in the room , capacities + pricing + regulation , all 3 determine industry profit pools

Aerospace: tier wise capability mapping that enables the company to participate with OEM's at a relationship level rather than a supplier level , if they have that depth and time they can deliver to the customer , it is a very difficult business to be in if you are a tier 1 player but also rewarding in the duopoly of commercial

These are some of the starting points that later become obvious when studying a business and now valuing them from aspects is another aspect that is more important , but must be remembered , otherwise you can follow Value Equity😃

RT ValueEquity
Businesses I was reading this week and found interesting across sectors, market sense note
(09/08/26)

1) Cohance Life Sciences: There seems to be something interesting happening here in terms of a possible turnaround, usually when private equity is involved, I don’t like it so much but in this case something seems interesting
Q1 was expected to be on the weaker side and just played out that way , now the management has guided for some really good incremental growth led by major opportunities in the commercial pipeline that start to deliver for them

Some context on them when things started to look interesting in early May this year , they hired Umang Vohra as the new Chairman and Group CEO , he was CFO at Dr.Reddy’s for North America , then global CEO and MD at Cipla and now moving his capability stack into a much smaller less than $2B company which is Cohance ( earlier suven run by Jasti Family and now sold their stake to Advent PE in 2023 )

Lets see what is happening now :
The company has a very high capability set in Anti Body Drug Conjugates payloads ( ADC payload linker bioconjugation, working with 3 large pharma innovators , with 10 molecules in phase 3 , RFQ’s almost doubled with good tailwinds and also Amongst few CDMOs globally specialized in Oligonucleotide and mRNA building blocks including specific delivery systems and Tri-cyclo-DNA
So capability wise they are pretty good, so if they are so good why are they not so successful?

Answer really lies in the NJ bio ADC platform ( spends far more then it earns ) , which is directly associated to the Biotech Funding winter in the US where there is lower funding activity from the peak , even though as written in my last note with some deals where Biotech M&A is very hot last month in the US >All of 2025 size , there are very large M&A deals happening in the pharma space in the US as well ( Vertex acquiring Crinetics for $10B , endocrine therapies rare disease pipeline ) , Eli Lily acquisition of AtaiBeckly ( $2.8B , Psychedelic medicines entry , very interesting as first for them) Chinese Biotechs rising on the Global front Astrazenca licensing Chinese technologies in Pharma with CPSC and more

This with a management transition happening often, better scope for plant compliance and few issues of molecules going off patent are few issues to name.
In fact one thing I liked here was Umang who just joined , honestly admitting on how they missed out on the opportunities that Laurus caught very well on engaging anchor clients , deepening relationships , scaling accounts and being an end to end player , he agreed that due to managements changing they did loose some focus on the larger tailwinds that were there, but now he wants to change that by re engaging this focus back on this and hence looking at scaling the business substantially with CDMO and Oligonucleotides and Nucleic acid building blocks
The thing I don’t like in private equity ownerships is they are always looking at that exit multiple peak story where it has now been 3 years to this from when Advent got in , I wont be surprised in the next 1-2 years there might be a stake sale again by advent like what Carlyle is doing in Sequent by “ creating value” by merging a high quality business like Viyash with Sequent

Now they are suggesting that they do see growth coming back post Q1 and this year H2 being good post which they expect to be on a sustained growth trajectory to reach an “aspirational “ target of $1B by 2030 , this is a story worth tracking on incremental execution pick up if they are able to deliver now with Umang Vohra heading this.

2) MV Electro systems : Interesting company to track , they make railway propulsion equipment is the product or equipment that makes trains move on tracks. It includes main parts like Converter-Inverter Systems, Vehicle Control System or Train Control Management System, Driver Displays. Propulsion provides the traction power needed to pull coaches and wagons over long distances.
Railway propulsion equipment is used across a wide range of applications. These include passenger trains such as metros, suburban rail, intercity trains, and high-speed rail, as well as freight trains that transport coal, steel, cement, containers, and other goods. They are also critical in urban rail systems like metros, monorails, and in specialized rail vehicles used in mining and heavy industries.
IGBT based 3-Phase Drive Propulsion equipment for electric locomotives, switchgear panels for railway coaches & EMU’s, cable protection & management products and electrical components, systems & sub-systems.
focused towards research, design & development of electrical equipment & power electronics systems for usage in railways industry and to play a strategic role as a domestic manufacturer with technical capabilities, indigenous designed and developed propulsion equipment and in-house assembling cum manufacturing facilities. The ingenious in-house design & development of 3-Phase Propulsion Equipment for 6000 HP Locomotive is a key achievement of our Company which will lead the way for us to create various other energy efficient railway power conversion systems. The transcript must clearly signal a shift from Santaap mode to Kantaap mode.
The playbook is simple. Enter in Santaap mode when pessimism is extreme, as seen in Laurus in 2019 and 2023.
What matters next is the emergence of capacity and capability that indicate a transition toward Kantaap mode. ROCE must be in Santaap (opposite to what Pulak Prasad looks for). That is where the highest alpha is made.

Neuland at one point traded at 0.5x sales and even in 2022 was only around 1.5x. ROCE used to be 4%
The opportunity lies in recognising when the narrative is about to change, not after it is obvious.

However, if Santaap persists without any improvement in capacity or capability, do not wait indefinitely. Cull decisively and redeploy capital. Walking away is always better than standing at a crash site hoping for recovery.

Shilpa was in full Santaap not so long ago; ROCE was bleeding; now heading into Kantaap zone; not there yet, but maybe as we exit FY28. Aim to visit their facilities shortly. There’s tremendous potential. No guarantee. Just optionality. Opportunity to scale up!

My upcoming India visit won’t have any investor meets. Multiple plant visits and meetings. Nothing else.

items.title: For years while economists both inside and outside China have called on Beijing to fight off delation and raise the consumption share of GDP by loweri...
items.description_html:
For years while economists both inside and outside China have called on Beijing to fight off delation and raise the consumption share of GDP by lowering interest rates and expanding credit, I have argued that this is the wrong solution, based on mistakenly assuming that China's financial system works like that of the US.

In fact it works in a very different way. Chinese banks mostly borrow from households to lend to businesses and government. Households are overwhelmingly net creditors to the banks while businesses and government net borrowers.

Lowering interest rates, in other words, rather mechanically reduces the household income share of GDP and expand the business and government shares, which means it tends to expand production faster than consumption.

We saw this most obviously in the 2000s, when Beijing engineered highly negative real interest rates to help clean up bad debt, and saw a near-collapse of the household share of GDP (and with it, the consumption share).

That's why, I argued, credit expansion and lower interest rates in China actually reduce consumption and are likely to be deflationary. This, by the way, was a similar story in Japan in the 1980s and 1990s.

Jinfan Zhang and Wei Xiong have just published an NBER paper that makes a very similar point. They write: "This paper investigates why China’s recurrent credit expansions have coincided with persistently weak inflation. We argue that this pattern reflects the country’s production-oriented monetary regime."

"Credit expansion in China," they continue, "tends to sustain production and balance sheets rather than stimulate final demand. As a result, monetary policy operates less as a conventional tool for demand management and durable reflation, and more as a mechanism for preserving production capacity and supporting growth."

If they are right (and I think they clearly are right), this has the seemingly counter-intuitive implication that rebalancing the economy towards a greater reliance on domestic consumption requires higher, not lower interest rates.

Of course given how heavily indebted government and businesses are, raising interest rates will be extremely painful for the production side of the economy, but this simply reinforces what we already know from the historical precedents – that it is necessary, but extremely painful, to rebalance an economy with very low consumption.

That's because the income transfers needed to rebalance an economy towards consumption must come from a production side that had previously benefitted from the reverse transfers. This almost always results in a growth contraction on the production side. That is probably why rebalancing is always put off for so long.

items.description_html:
RT Ananth Rupanagudi
Early 20th Century, Tiruttangal (Thiruthangal), Madras Presidency. Map of India Before Partition - Vintage Matchbox Art. Thiruthangal is still known for its printing, match-works and fireworks industries.

Hindusthan Match Industries (often labelled as Hindusthan Match Industries, Sivakasi/Tiruttangal) was a classic mid-20th-century safety match manufacturer based in the Madras Presidency (now Tamil Nadu), operating out of the Sivakasi-Tiruttangal region—the historical capital and backbone of India's non-mechanized match production.

Following World War I and the Swadeshi movement, local entrepreneurs in Tamil Nadu—particularly around Sivakasi, Kovilpatti, and Sattur—traveled to hubs like Calcutta (where early match production began around 1910) to learn match-making techniques.

Factories like Hindusthan Match Industries emerged during the British era as part of a flourishing localized cottage and semi-automated industry. The dry climate, affordable labour, and access to softwoods made Tamil Nadu the premier location for scaling manual and semi-automatic match production. #matchbox #industry #history

items.description_html:
Wall Street is paying less attention to the Magnificent 7:

Monthly mentions of the "Magnificent Seven" across news stories on the Bloomberg terminal are down to ~1,400, near the lowest since Q4 2023.

This marks a -70% decline from the Q1 2024 peak of ~4,300 mentions, which came shortly after the term was introduced in 2023.

A similar pattern occurred with the "FANG" and later "FAANG" labels, originally referring to Facebook, Amazon, Netflix, and Google before Apple was added.

Monthly mentions of "FANG" and "FAANG" surged to a record ~2,800 in Q4 2018.

items.description_html:
BREAKING: China’s central bank officially added +20 tonnes of gold in July, its largest monthly purchase since October 2023.

This follows +15 tonnes and +10 tonnes acquired in June and May, respectively, and marks their 21st consecutive monthly increase in gold reserves.

Year-to-date, China has officially raised its gold reserves by +60 tonnes, bringing its total gold holdings up to a record 2,366 tonnes.

Meanwhile, China’s central bank has reportedly been moving more of its gold reserves from London to Hong Kong, signaling support for the city’s push to become a major global gold-trading hub.

The relocation is set to continue as Hong Kong launches a new gold-clearing system aimed at making the city a bigger center for global gold trading and pricing.

China’s appetite for gold remains incredibly strong.

items.description_html:
Record highs are back. What comes next?

The S&P 500 has risen in 13 of the last 17 instances following a significant breakout to an all-time high over the last 30 years.

During these periods, the index gained an average of ~6.3% over the subsequent 6 months.

The 4 exceptions came in 2000, 2007, 2018, and 2019, with the first two preceding major bear markets.

Most recently, in 2025, the S&P 500 gained +12.3% in the 6 months following a similar move to an all-time high.

Meanwhile, the S&P 500 has posted 26 all-time highs in 2026, following 39 record closes in full-year 2025 and 57 in 2024.

History suggests market momentum is set to continue.

items.description_html:
South Korean retail investors are turning to US stocks amid domestic market turmoil:

Retail investors from South Korea bought +$4.6 billion worth of US stocks in July, the largest monthly total since January 2026.

This marks a +627% MoM increase and follows -$469 million and -$940 million in sales in April and May, respectively.

July purchases were also well above the +$2.7 billion monthly average recorded in 2025, a year when South Korean retail investors more than tripled their purchases of US equities from 2024.

As a result, South Korean retail investors bought more US stocks last month than domestic equities for the first time since February.

This comes as the KOSPI Index has dropped -33% from its June peak, with ~75% of the decline driven by the 2 largest chipmakers, Samsung and SK Hynix.

US stocks are benefiting from South Korea's market downturn.

items.title: Investors are worried about Big Tech's debt. Oracle's, $ORCL, 5-year credit default swap (CDS) has surged +70 basis points year-to-date, to a record ~...
items.description_html:
Investors are worried about Big Tech's debt.

Oracle's, $ORCL, 5-year credit default swap (CDS) has surged +70 basis points year-to-date, to a record ~215 basis points, the largest increase among Big Tech companies.

This is followed by Broadcom, $AVGO, whose 5-year CDS has risen +48 basis points over the same period.

Meta’s, $META, 5-year CDS is up +39 basis points, to 95 basis points, the highest since trading began in October 2025.

Nvidia's, $NVDA, 5-year CDS is up +32 basis points so far in 2026 to ~82 basis points, the highest since it began trading in November 2025.

Furthermore, the 5-year CDS for Amazon, $AMZN, and Alphabet, $GOOGL, has increased +30 and +29 basis points, respectively.

This comes as Big Tech companies have issued ~$200 billion in corporate bonds year-to-date, nearly double the full-year total for 2025.

Credit markets are becoming increasingly worried about the cost of financing the AI race.

items.description_html:
US crude oil inventories are experiencing an unprecedented decline:

Total US crude oil inventories have fallen for 17 consecutive weeks, the longest streak on record.

This surpasses the previous record of 16-straight weekly declines seen in 2021.

Since early April, total crude oil inventories have plunged -166 million barrels, to 712 million barrels, the lowest since March 1984.

The Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) alone has dropped -111 million barrels since March, to 305 million barrels, the lowest since February 1983.

Meanwhile, excluding the SPR, US oil inventories have fallen for 10 consecutive weeks, matching the 2018 record streak.

US oil supplies are experiencing a historic decline.

items.title: I think John Burn-Murdoch is right: "The most durable way for governments to ensure that both university students and their less academic counterparts...
items.description_html:
I think John Burn-Murdoch is right: "The most durable way for governments to ensure that both university students and their less academic counterparts can move through the education system confident of good financial outcomes for themselves is to have a dynamic economy and robust productivity growth."

You hear all sorts of silly arguments that China has a strong manufacturing sector because its universities produce engineers, where American universities produces lawyers, but this is the same sort of silliness we heard about Japan in the 1980s, and, just as it did then, it gets the causality backwards.

Chinese students – like Japanese students in the 1980s, Germans in the 2000s and Americans in the 1950s and 1960s – major in engineering because, thanks to the tremendous support its government gives to the manufacturing and high-tech sectors, that is where the best jobs are. If the UK and the US want the same, instead of prioritizing finance and services, they should prioritize manufacturing. Once the opportunities are there, the students will follow.

items.description_html:
There seems to be a growing acknowledgement around the word that Keynes was right when he proposed at Bretton Woods a global trading regime that limited persistent trade imbalances and restricted global financial flows.

In her new Foreign Affairs piece, Lori Wallach proposes a similar restructuring of the global trading regime, arguing that because our current trading system rewards countries that improve their manufacturing competitiveness by suppressing wage growth relative to productivity growth (and by ignoring environmental costs), it's no surprise that income inequality has risen across most countries over the past four decades.

Like a growing number of analysts, she argues that countries should be free to choose their own growth models, but they should not be able to externalize the associated costs via their trade and capital accounts.

items.title: In the Indian CDMO landscape, what we saw in the first phase was discovery services, followed by tech transfers for late-stage commercial manufacturin...
items.description_html:
In the Indian CDMO landscape, what we saw in the first phase was discovery services, followed by tech transfers for late-stage commercial manufacturing.

What is being seen now is a migration into the middle part i.e FTE collaboration where WuXi held all the relationships, and this is starting to shift here to India.

Why this matters:

1) Discovery chemistry :- early-stage medicinal chemistry, custom synthesis support. Low ticket size per molecule, but this is where you capture a molecule first.

2) FTE development/collaboration (the middle) :- dedicated scientist teams billed on a time-and-materials basis, doing process development, route scouting, and scale-up as a molecule moves through Phase I/II/III. This is iterative, relationship-heavy work, not a fixed-fee deliverable.

3) Commercial manufacturing :- large-scale API/intermediate production post-approval.

WuXi's edge was never any single stage; rather, it was owning the relationship through the middle, so molecules they touched in discovery naturally migrated to them for commercial manufacturing later. India's first wave (Divi's, Laurus, etc.) largely won stage 3 via tech-transfer on already-late-stage molecules, skipping the relationship capture. Discovery-stage players (Syngene, Sai Life's own discovery arm, Antherm) won stage 1 in isolation.

The gap has been the FTE middle, and that's what Sai Life is now saying it's building out. Owning it means:

(a) Higher stickiness :- once you're embedded in a client's development work, you follow the molecule to commercial scale rather than losing it to a tech-transfer competitor; and

(b) Better economics :- FTE billing during development typically carries better margins than late-stage generic API work.

But this is very early-stage development, and it remains to be seen how things move from here.

Disclaimer - not a recommendation to buy/sell

items.title: I want to revisit the Philanthropic 11 today, but not as a victory lap. What interests me is what I was actually thinking on 16 September 2022, when n...
items.description_html:
I want to revisit the Philanthropic 11 today, but not as a victory lap.

What interests me is what I was actually thinking on 16 September 2022, when none of us knew how the next few years would play out. It is very easy to look backwards at a successful investment and construct a beautiful thesis around the outcome. I don't want to do that.

The batting order tells a more honest story.

Neuland was my Sehwag, and Syngene was my Tendulkar.

They were the two openers.

Laurus was batting at number 9.

That was not accidental. The order reflected my conviction at the time and, equally importantly, the risks I thought each business had to navigate.

I had a strong conviction on Neuland. The prevailing sentiment was deeply pessimistic, but I thought the eventual outcome could be almost diagonally opposite. I believed the innovator synthesis business had the potential to compound meaningfully as more NCEs moved towards commercialisation. I wrote at the time that I was a biased bull on “Neuland Deuterated Labs” and expected a significant improvement in perception between FY22 and FY27.

So Neuland was Sehwag.

Aggressive. Unfashionable at the time. And a player I thought could change the game.

Syngene was different.

I saw it as a great player who was temporarily out of form. The franchise was strong, the relationships were strong and the CRO track record was impressive.

Class is permanent. Form is temporary.

That was my thinking. FYI @kiranshaw

The Mangalore API facility was approaching US FDA approval, and I saw that as an important milestone before a potential increase in throughput. I extrapolated Syngene's excellent CRO track record into the emerging commercial-scale CDMO opportunity.

This is where I have to be honest with myself.

My due diligence was not good enough.

I gave too much weight to the smooth management narrative and the CRO track record when thinking about a different and more difficult proposition: commercial-scale small-molecule CDMO manufacturing.

That was my mistake.

And I don't want to hide it behind hindsight.

Laurus was number 9 for a completely different reason.

I had reasonable long-term conviction in Laurus, but I expected it to suffer first. The earlier USD 1 billion guidance was, in my view, ill-timed and had no real support in my thinking model. More importantly, the extraordinary COVID-era Paxlovid opportunity was about to unwind.

The collapse of that purchase order was going to hit the Laurus system.

So I did not put Laurus alongside Neuland as an opener. I put it at number 9.

That did not mean I had low conviction in Laurus over the long term. It meant I expected the business to go through pain before earning its place in the team.

Several months later, in mid-2023, I doubled down on Laurus when the stock and the narrative had acquired much of the negativity and pessimism that Neuland had carried in 2022.

If I had created the playing 11 then (mid-2023), Laurus would have opened alongside Neuland. Syngene would not have been the opener.

This is why I want to preserve the original batting order rather than rewrite history around what happened subsequently.

The Philanthropic 11 was a decision made in September 2022. It reflected what I knew, what I believed and, importantly, what I did not know.

Syngene was my wrong judgement.

And that wrong judgement has probably been more useful to me than many of my correct ones.

The shock of what happened with Syngene has acted like a shock on the Hydra.

It forced a system change.

Today, I demand much more evidence before allowing a smooth narrative, an impressive track record or management confidence to influence my conviction. I want evidence that connects what a company has actually demonstrated in the past with what I am assuming it can do in the future.

The suffering Syngene gave me in 2022 has made my decision system stronger.

That is the part of Taleb's Hydra that I find most interesting. The objective isn't to build a system that never gets things wrong. That is impossible.

The objective is to make sure that when reality proves you wrong, the system comes back stronger.

If I were to create a fresh philanthropic 11 today, I would obviously hope the new team has a higher probability of beating the market. But the more important point is that the system selecting that team is stronger today than it was in 2022.

And there is one more thing I want to make clear.

A playing 11 is what the team management decides on the day.

The pitch changes. The weather changes. The opposition changes. A player's form changes. Sometimes our understanding of the player changes.

Investment is no different.

When conditions outside the system change, we must have the courage to change the batting order. When our understanding of the business changes, we must have the humility to change it too.

Moving Laurus from number 9 to number 1 is not an inconsistency if the evidence has changed.

Keeping it at number 9 simply because that was the original decision would be stubbornness.

And keeping Syngene at number 2 because I once called it Tendulkar would be even worse. It would mean becoming attached to my own narrative.

Conviction should give us the courage to act, but it should never take away the flexibility to change our minds.

That is why I want to revisit these three stocks.

Neuland was Sehwag because I saw something the prevailing sentiment did not.

Syngene was Tendulkar because I believed a great player was temporarily out of form. I got that judgement wrong, and that mistake forced a change in my system.

Laurus was number 9 because I believed the long-term player would first have to go through a difficult phase. When the conditions changed, I changed the batting order.

There is no hindsight here. At least, that is what I am trying hard to avoid.

The real objective is not to have a perfect record. It is to make sure that every serious mistake makes the decision-making system harder to fool the next time.

That is the Hydra I am trying to become.

items.title: RT Pratik Bhakta: ‼️UPI growth is slowing down ‼️ One of the biggest concerns for the digital payments industry right now is around penetration of...
items.description_html:
RT Pratik Bhakta
‼️UPI growth is slowing down ‼️

One of the biggest concerns for the digital payments industry right now is around penetration of UPI payments.

Data for the last five years show that UPI growth has slowed down drastically.

Though there is definitely a base effect that is kicking in.

UPI penetration is still less than 50% of the country. So there is enough room to grow quickly.

Ask industry insiders and they will say that penetration is slowing down, new user addition into the UPI ecosystem is slowing down too.

And ask why?

They will all point fingers towards MDR, no revenue on UPI payments, hence banks and fintechs are not investing in growth.

Amrish Rau, CEO, Pine Labs pointed this out recently in his tweet. UPI penetration is still around 35-40%, while digital payments penetration in Brazil and China is above 90%.

Now as the government is finally opening up to bringing back MDR and the Finance Ministry is supporting the move, lets hope growth comes back to digital payments.

Layoffs across the information sector are accelerating:

The layoff rate in the information sector jumped +0.7 percentage points in June, to 2.3%, the 3rd-highest since the 2020 pandemic.

This means that ~2.3% of employees in the sector were laid off or discharged during the month.

Since November 2025, the layoff rate has more than doubled.

In absolute terms, 63,000 workers were laid off or discharged in June, the 3rd-highest monthly total since April 2020.

As a result, the 6-month moving average layoff rate rose to 2.0%, the 2nd-highest on record.

By comparison, this metric peaked at ~1.5% during the 2008 Financial Crisis and the 2001 recession.

AI continues to transform the labor market.

items.title: US productivity growth is accelerating: US labor productivity rose +1.4% annualized rate in Q2 2026, more than double the +0.6% expected. This follows...
items.description_html:
US productivity growth is accelerating:

US labor productivity rose +1.4% annualized rate in Q2 2026, more than double the +0.6% expected.

This follows an upwardly revised +0.8% increase in Q1, marking the 5th consecutive quarter of productivity gains.

At the same time, US manufacturing productivity jumped +1.9%, driven by a +4.6% surge in output, the strongest increase since Q4 2021.

However, these productivity gains came at the expense of workers, with inflation-adjusted compensation falling -3.2%, the largest quarterly decline since Q4 2022.

Meanwhile, unit labor costs, which measure how much a company pays workers to produce one unit of output, rose just +1.3% last quarter, well below the +2.1% expected.

The productivity boom is gaining momentum.

Urban Company was running two models side by side: the beauty services business on a full-stack model in cities like Gurgaon, Bengaluru and Mumbai, while most other categories continued as an open marketplace.

On the supply side, professionals started coming to Urban Company on their own for the first time.

Customer cohorts were improving, and retention was significantly better for the full-stack beauty business.

In WhatsApp groups, customers started referring to it as "the beauty app."

"Initially, that was a little unsettling because we offered so many different services," says co-founder and CEO Abhiraj Bhal.

"But I realised that this was the only category where we were truly solving the customer's problem end to end."

That was the turning point.

items.title: US refiners have shifted away from Saudi oil: US imports of Saudi Arabian crude fell to zero in July, marking the first full month without imports sin...
items.description_html:
US refiners have shifted away from Saudi oil:

US imports of Saudi Arabian crude fell to zero in July, marking the first full month without imports since 1985, according to preliminary US government data.

This marks a sharp reversal from March, when US refiners were purchasing more than 800,000 barrels of Saudi crude oil per day.

This comes as US refiners sought alternative supplies after the closure of the Strait of Hormuz and broader Iran War-related disruptions pushed Middle Eastern crude prices higher.

As a result, Venezuela has emerged as the primary replacement, with US imports of its crude surging to ~600,000 barrels per day in July, up from just ~100,000 barrels per day at the start of the year.

Global oil trade flows are undergoing a historic shift.

items.description_html:
RT Mark Zandi
There’s no sugar coating the overarching message in the July jobs report – the economy is struggling. Job growth is at a virtual standstill, and concentrated in a few sectors. While unemployment is low, that’s only because those losing their jobs are leaving the workforce, too discouraged to look for a job, as few businesses are hiring. Hours worked are low and are slumping lower. Wage growth continues to decelerate and is below the rate of inflation, a clear tell that the job market is operating below full-employment despite the low unemployment rate. No wonder most Americans say they are upset about their finances and the economy’s performance.

items.title: One of my objectives as an investor is to keep learning from business leaders and other investors, in public as well as in private. Over the years, I ...
items.description_html:
One of my objectives as an investor is to keep learning from business leaders and other investors, in public as well as in private.

Over the years, I have also learnt to listen differently.

What someone says matters. But how they say it, what they choose not to say, and how much they need you to believe them can sometimes tell you just as much.

Earlier this year, Neuland Labs was meeting investors at a large institutional conference in London. Some of the biggest FIIs met the team, and I had the opportunity to join some of those meetings.

That made the setting particularly interesting to observe.

When sophisticated investors are sitting across the table asking detailed questions, there is always an opportunity for management to become a little more expansive than it is in public. A slightly stronger adjective. A little more colour around the pipeline. A hint about what might be coming. Nothing explicit enough to be called guidance, but enough to make the listener leave the room feeling better about the story.

I saw none of that.

The team did not guide beyond what it had already communicated publicly. There was no attempt to make the opportunity sound bigger, no effort to impress the room, and remarkably little interest in selling the fundamentals.

The tone, if I had to describe it, was simply:

This is what it is. This is what we know. This is what we can tell you. See if it fits your process.

What made this observation meaningful to me, however, wasn't that particular conference.

My interactions with Team Neuland go back years and span very different levels of the organisation, from plant operators and middle management to senior leadership.

Different people. Different settings. Different years.

Yet there has been a certain consistency in behaviour.

And I increasingly find consistency across levels of an organisation more revealing than a polished interaction with its senior management.

People reveal themselves through what they say, but also through what they feel compelled to project. The need to persuade, impress, forecast or constantly reinforce a narrative can itself be information.

So can the absence of that need.

There is an asymmetry here that I find particularly important.

A company may gain something small by making its story sound a little better in a private room. But it risks something much larger if its words begin to differ depending on who happens to be sitting across the table.

Trust compounds slowly. It can disappear very quickly.

Restraint, therefore, can be information too.

None of this tells me what Neuland's earnings will be next quarter. It doesn't tell me what the stock should be worth. And it certainly doesn't mean execution cannot disappoint.

Behaviour should never substitute for numbers, competitive analysis or valuation.

Behaviour is evidence, not proof.

But after years of interacting with businesses, there is one question I increasingly find myself asking:

How badly do these people need me to believe their story?

My interactions with Team Neuland over the years, from plant operators to middle and senior management, have repeatedly left me with the impression that they don't.

They seem quite comfortable letting you make up your own mind.

Sometimes, what a business feels no need to sell you tells you something about the business itself.

items.title: Li Daokui: "The overall judgment is that new drivers of growth have not yet been created, while the old growth engines of recent decades have already ...
items.description_html:
Li Daokui: "The overall judgment is that new drivers of growth have not yet been created, while the old growth engines of recent decades have already faded."

"Over the past 20 years," he continues, "China’s rapid economic expansion was driven primarily not by household consumption—whose share of GDP was roughly 35 to 38 percent, excluding services consumption—but by two major engines. The first was the largest infrastructure buildout in human history. The second was the broad upswing in real estate."

Many people are talking about this July 12 speech by Li Daokui, not because his analysis is especially new (many Chinese economists have been saying similar things privately, just as many foreign economists have been saying them publicly), but because he said it in such a public forum.

Even as he insists several times that "China's future is very bright," as he probably must, the speech nonetheless suggests that we may be seeing a gradual shift in the policymaking consensus.

To me, the most important part of the speech is his willingness to state clearly something that I don't think Beijing wants to hear. There is a hope among policymakers that over the next few years Beijing will manage a transition in which the healthy part of the K-shaped economy (advanced technology and high-value-added manufacturing) becomes sufficiently strong relative to the weak part (everything else) to pull the whole economy forward.

In my opinion, this was always unlikely, even in a world willing to absorb China's attempt to expand its already-large global share of advanced technology and high-value-added manufacturing. In today's world of rising trade tensions, however, I think it is all but impossible. Only the United States, the European Union, and Japan are large enough and advanced enough to support China's manufacturing ambitions through their net demand, and all three are increasingly closing their markets.

Li seems to agree that this "K-shaped dream" is unrealistic. He says: "Once we start talking about K-shaped divergence, it is as though we are placing our hopes on the upward arm of the K and expecting it to pull the entire Chinese economy forward. That actually leads us away from the real problem. The upper arm of the K cannot pull up the entire economic base. On this issue, we must maintain a strong sense of urgency."

While I agree strongly with Li's analysis of the problem, however, I disagree with his solution, which is to use the central government balance sheet to clean up local government balance sheets so that they can return to their old mission of pumping up economic activity. "The crux of the problem," he says, "is the blockage, and the blockage lies in local-government debt. The answer is therefore obvious: the central government, and indeed the public sector as a whole, should expand its debt level."

My problem with this proposal is that it assumes local governments invested badly for reasons that can be corrected. It further assumes that future behavior can be changed, perhaps by requiring local governments to promise to reform: "Eligible local governments could apply to the central government and sign a commitment promising to regulate future borrowing and refrain from excessive debt issuance, in exchange for replacing their existing high-interest debt."

But that is not what happened, nor is it what will happen. Beijing has set excessively high GDP growth targets for decades. Because it could not get consumption growth to accelerate sufficiently, this meant that it also could not allow investment growth to decelerate. With the highest investment rates in history, achieving these growth targets required an enormous pipeline of economically viable investment projects.

The problem is that, unlike the period before the end of the 2000s, China is no longer sufficiently underinvested across the board for huge increases in investment to generate enough viable projects and sustain real growth.

China has had excess capacity in property, infrastructure, and manufacturing for many years. That necessarily means the returns on new investment have been very low or even negative. And because investment remained so high, debt had to surge – which, of course, it did. Not only has this problem not improved in recent years, it has become progressively worse.

That is why local-government debt has risen so much faster since the early 2010s than the real value of provincial economies. That is why so many provinces are struggling under their debt burdens. It is not that local governments were careless or irresponsible when they made these investments. Rather, the GDP growth targets themselves forced them to continue investing, whether or not additional investment was economically justified. The inevitable result was an ever-growing volume of non-productive investment.

Because provinces are now burdened by these debts, Li proposes cleaning up their balance sheets by transferring the debt onto the central government balance sheet. He is right that the central government still has a relatively clean balance sheet. It is, in fact, the last clean balance sheet left in China.

But that is precisely why I think it should not be compromised in an effort to sustain GDP growth targets that have become increasingly unrealistic for an economy facing the kinds of structural problems Li himself describes.

As long as Beijing continues to set excessively high GDP growth targets, there is no way to prevent debt from continuing to surge. My concern is that Li's proposal would simply cause China to lose the last clean balance sheet it still possesses and, with it, its ability to moderate and manage the pace of what is likely to be an inevitable – and inevitably difficult – adjustment.
https://sinocism.notion.site/Li-Daokui-China-s-Biggest-Economic-Problem-Is-Not-K-Shaped-Divergence-but-an-Economy-That-Is-Cold--3b484ece41d78174b379f9243c605575

"The outlook, however, is hazy because of the uncertainties regarding south-west monsoon, El Niño, geopolitics and global trade policy. items.title: Bloomberg on Russia's version of Dutch disease: "Instead of oil revenues pulling workers and capital into the energy sector while hollowing out the re...
items.description_html:
Bloomberg on Russia's version of Dutch disease: "Instead of oil revenues pulling workers and capital into the energy sector while hollowing out the rest of the economy, massive military spending is drawing them into defense industries, pushing up labor costs and steadily eroding the competitiveness of civilian businesses."

In a closed economic system, like the global economy, rising wages may be painful for businesses in the short term, but as Michael Kalecki explianed, over the longer term they are not a bad thing. By driving demand for production and by creating incentives for businesses to invest in productivity-enhancing technology, they result in faster production growth that ultimately accommodates not only higher wages but also higher profits.

A problem for Russia (and for other countries that try to raise wages) is that it is a part of a badly-globalized economic system, one in which countries are globally competitive in manufacturing mainly to the extent that they are able to suppress wage growth relative to productivity growth.

When wages in an economy grow relative the productivity, in other words, that may be good for global demand and for global growth, but it makes that economy less competitive in manufacturing, sending more than 100% of the benefits of higher wages to manufacturing to its trade partners.

Russia thus faces the double economic problem not just of an incredibly expensive war, but of rising wages which will further undermine its already-struggling manufacturing sector for the benefit of its trade partners.

Russia is not the example that I would have normally used, but it nonetheless illustrates an important point: the global economy would be much better off with a trade and capital regime that rewards economies that raise wages rather than punish them.
https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-06/russia-s-war-economy-is-fueling-pay-gains-companies-can-t-afford?srnd=phx-economics-v2

items.title: RT Steven N. Durlauf: The treatment of Sanjay Reddy @sanjaygreddy is disgraceful. He is a key figure in the Economics Department of the New School and...
items.description_html:
RT Steven N. Durlauf
The treatment of Sanjay Reddy @sanjaygreddy is disgraceful. He is a key figure in the Economics Department of the New School and is one of the most trenchant critiques of neoclassical economics anywhere. I profoundly disagree with most of what he has to say, but that is of no importance. What is important is that that he is a key thinker on the limits of mainstream economics. To the extent that this action inhibits his future contributions, the discipline is the poorer.

More broadly developments at The New School are terrible news for the academy. The New School's championship of heterodox thinking and scholarly dissent has played and plays a unique role in the ecology of knowledge creation for economics and for social science.

The treatment of Sanjay Reddy @sanjaygreddy is disgraceful. He is a key figure in the Economics Department and one of the most trenchant critiques of neoclassical economics anywhere. I profoundly disagree with most of what he has to say, but that is the point. To the extent that this action inhibits his future contributions, the discipline is the poorer.

He who knows only his own side of the case, knows little of that. His reasons may be good, and no one may have been able to refute them. But if he is equally unable to refute the reasons on the opposite side; if he does not so much as know what they are, he has no ground for preferring either opinion...Nor is it enough that he should hear the arguments of adversaries from his own teachers, presented as they state them, and accompanied by what they offer as refutations. That is not the way to do justice to the arguments, or bring them into real contact with his own mind. He must be able to hear them from persons who actually believe them; who defend them in earnest, and do their very utmost for them.

John Stuart Mill, On LibertyCrisis at The New School@TheNewSchool

items.title: RT Pavel Durov: Last night Apple briefly removed Telegram from the AppStore because a user had planted illegal porn in a public chat. Telegram was res...
items.description_html:
RT Pavel Durov
Last night Apple briefly removed Telegram from the AppStore because a user had planted illegal porn in a public chat.

Telegram was restored within hours. But I want to explain what happened — to warn other app developers and help protect online communities from similar attacks.

Because Telegram quickly removes illegal content from public groups using all kinds of moderation tools, the attacker had to resort to a technical trick. He inserted AI-modified illegal content by editing an old message in an active group chat. As a result the content was effectively hidden from the group’s members, preventing them from seeing/reporting it.

The attacker was a takedown extortionist: someone who demands ransom from group owners in exchange for not targeting their communities. These extortionists use automated accounts to plant illegal content in public groups and then report it directly to Apple, attempting to trigger the removal of legitimate communities whose owners refused to pay them.

From a practical standpoint, illegal pornographic content in Telegram’s public groups is not a systemic problem. Our moderation is effective. The fact that attackers must resort to backdated, effectively invisible content and other technical tricks proves this.

⚠️ However, there are two important lessons here for app developers and online communities:

— Extortionists have found a way to manipulate Apple into overreacting. Apple removed Telegram from the App Store before contacting us. This creates a potential systemic risk for every mobile app that hosts user-generated content. If an app used by more than a billion people can be removed from the App Store without prior warning, any app can be.

— The tactics used by takedown extortionists are evolving, putting communities across social platforms at risk. Telegram has extensive experience identifying the tricks used by coordinated reporting gangs and protecting legitimate communities (even when doing so risks our own app being temporarily removed from the App Store). Other platforms may not be equally prepared.

Stay vigilant! ☝️

Arbitrage funds recorded their highest daily return (~0.50%) in history by delivering 8–10 times their average daily returns (~0.05%)

UTI Arbitrage Fund : +0.40%
Tata Arbitrage Fund : 0.43%
SBI Arbitrage Fund : +0.51%
Edelweiss Arb Fund : +0.45%
ICICI Arbitrage Fund : +0.44%
Kotak Arbitrage Fund : +0.48%
HDFC Arbitrage Fund : +0.53%
Aditya Birla Arb Fund : +0.48%
Nippon India Arb Fund : +0.48%
Invesco Arbitrage Fund : +0.42%

7 of 10 funds recorded their highest daily percentage gain in the last decade on the first day of the Closing Auction Session

These funds saw a very rare rise in their net asset values across the category, averaging 0.46%. This was about 7.3 standard deviations higher than their usual daily movement

items.title: RT Vinay Kesari: Good move, and hope it succeeds! Reality check: This amendment would create an *enabling mechanism* to more easily tweak MDR structur...
items.description_html:
RT Vinay Kesari
Good move, and hope it succeeds!

Reality check: This amendment would create an *enabling mechanism* to more easily tweak MDR structure on UPI and RuPay. Any actual change in MDR would have to come via a separate govt. notification under the PSSA (simpler than an amendment to a law), of which there isn't visibility yet.

Why it's still encouraging: It seems unlikely that time would be spent on such an amendment unless there is real intention to tweak MDR structure. UPI subsidy to payments players has been sharply declining (down ~50% since 2023-24) despite the massive growth in UPI and attendant increase in costs. It is inevitable that these costs have to at least be offset if there is to be continued healthy growth of UPI.

What form this could take: Reintroduction of MDR on UPI and RuPay debit txns for 'large merchants' (which industry has been pushing for) is a possible pragmatic path, preserving the benefits of widespread digital acceptance by small merchants while placing the onus on larger merchants to pay for the benefit of frictionless payments.

Qns. to think about: 1. If the eventual notification imposes MDR on txns>Rs.2,000 at large merchants, which payments players would benefit the most in the short term?

2. If the costs related to UPI acceptance for large merchants goes up, it narrows the gap with accepting credit instruments. Could this incentivise more merchant-funded checkout finance?


Pratik Bhakta: Govt is planning to introduce an ammendment to the Payment and Settlement System Act, 2007 thtough Bill no 150 of 2026.

This might pave the way for the RBI to re-impose MDR on RuPay debit cards and UPI.

Sources say bill might be introduced in the Parliament tomorrow.

“The best thing the U.S. government has done on immigration is OPT to allow international students a chance to stay and work for a time after graduation.”

OPT gave her the opportunity to refine “the business plan that helped create the company."

Charging a $100k fee on OPT would nuke a critical pathway for recruiting & retaining global talent.

A $100,000 fee on OPT would have lost us many of them.

Founders like these would be eligible for an O-1 today, after they've built their companies. But not when they were getting started.

items.title: There's a lot of discussion about Energy Security. Not enough about Edible oil security. India imports 60% of all our seed oils, and 90% of Palm oils ...
items.description_html:
There's a lot of discussion about Energy Security. Not enough about Edible oil security. India imports 60% of all our seed oils, and 90% of Palm oils (mainly from Malaysia and Indonesia). The largest agri-economy has yet to secure its kitchen oils.

Both Indonesia and Malaysia are now levying export curbs and increasing domestic palm oil blending mandates for domestic energy production. Indonesia is already transitioning from B30 to mandatory B40 and planned B50 biodiesel blending, reducing global export availability. Malaysia is similarly expanding domestic palm oil blending mandates.

Bottomline: There is a massive shift amongst countries towards reducing crude oil imports and blending is the way forward. Ethanol in India, Crude Palm oil (CPO) for them.

Indonesia’s palm oil curbs could open the door for India to step up. What was earlier just an agri-policy (National Mission on Edible Oils) will soon be National priority. And unlike Energy security which is more challenging, this is an easier to solve problem. The acceleration is visible. Telangana and AP have championed the India Palm Oil mission, many more states are coming up now.

Which company fills the void? That's for investors to figure out. A good opportunity in the making.

Read:
https://www.fortuneindia.com/opinion/indonesias-palm-oil-curbs-could-open-the-door-for-india-to-step-up/150389

items.title: The AI memory crash comes on the back of last quarter record profits. Samsung chip division's single-year profits beat its past 40 years total profit....
items.description_html:
The AI memory crash comes on the back of last quarter record profits.

Samsung chip division's single-year profits beat its past 40 years total profit. Last quarter > Last 2 years. Stock has halved in a month.

Micron grew profits by 1400%, stock down 40-45%. Projections talk of record numbers for next 2 years as well. TTM PE hardly 4-5x.

So, why the panic and correction?

1. One obvious reason is profit booking, with record leverage in system amplifying the fall. What unfolded the sell-off was fear - China's Open source model and DRAM buildup fears, bond market pressure etc.

2. The other is valuation mistake. Is trailing P/E the right metric for extraordinary earnings cycle? The risks are in future, not in trail. The lesser variables you have that can impact earnings visibility the better. Here, there are more than what an analyst can predict with confidence.

Is this a buying opportunity? Is there more correction left? I don't know. But I know that basing investment decision solely on the fall from peak is often a mistake.

#FearandGreed

items.title: Ten Important Filings that you should know, for week ended 24th July 🌯 All data via https://thewrap.in 1. HFCL to expand Data Centre Connectivity c...
items.description_html:
Ten Important Filings that you should know, for week ended 24th July 🌯

All data via https://thewrap.in

1. HFCL to expand Data Centre Connectivity capacity by nearly 5x

HFCL will invest ₹215 crore to add capacity for 270,000 MMC and SNMT assemblies annually, with commissioning expected by September 2027

The capex represents a significant scale up while also shifting HFCL toward higher value connectivity products used inside AI and hyperscale data centers

https://www.bseindia.com/xml-data/corpfiling/AttachHis/7677aa47-7778-42cc-8404-83ff35875284.pdf

2. Paras Defence has signed a MoU to set up advanced packaging OSAT facility at cost of 6200cr

Advanced packaging is one of the crucial bottlenecks in AI supply chain today. TSMC overflow is already benefiting companies like ASE Tech and Amkor

Paras wants to set up latest 2.5D/3D advanced packaging line

This is just a MoU at this stage and no funding and terms have been finalized

https://www.bseindia.com/xml-data/corpfiling/AttachHis/f78828b7-aedc-4412-a05f-33fafd4aaefb.pdf

3. SPEL Semiconductor plans major expansion and fundraising of up to ₹1,000 crore

SPEL has approved raising up to ₹500 crore through a Rights Issue/QIP and another ₹500 crore through overseas instruments including FDI or FCCBs

SPEL currently operates a semiconductor packaging and testing facility, it does not manufacture chips or wafers

It packages fabricated semiconductor dies into finished ICs and performs electrical and reliability testing

The funds will be used to modernize and expand its packaging, testing, automation and manufacturing infrastructure
The company also plans to apply for Central and State semiconductor incentives

https://www.bseindia.com/xml-data/corpfiling/AttachHis/90be6dd5-03e3-4a54-a9c0-a4ba4a1f8183.pdf

4. ICE Make enters into a joint venture with Japanese company Galilei to foray into HoReCa segment

Galilei will also invest 180cr in ICE Make via preference shares

Food Processing & Hospitality already contributes 15-20% of ICE Make’s revenue, while commercial freezers account for only 2%, leaving significant headroom to build a larger standardized HoReCa equipment business

Galilei brings established Japanese product technology and has around 30% share of Japan’s domestic commercial-refrigerator production

https://nsearchives.nseindia.com/corporate/ICEMAKE_24072026125113_Outcome_of_Board_Meeting_final_2.pdf

5. Apollo Micro Systems receives Indian Navy approval to develop an Autonomous Underwater Surveillance System

Apollo Micro Systems has received a Make-II Prototype Sanction Order to develop SAVIOR-ASW, an unmanned semi-submersible vessel that can operate for extended periods and use acoustic sensors and AI/ML to detect and classify submarines and other underwater threats

The system would represent a first-of-its-kind indigenous capability in India and marks Apollo’s formal entry into autonomous maritime and underwater warfare systems

https://www.bseindia.com/xml-data/corpfiling/AttachHis/408de015-8d30-40a5-9dc6-87c5bc839242.pdf

6. Marine Electricals wins orders worth 376cr including a major order from Siemens for power distribution system that will be used in a Hyperscaler data center

https://nsearchives.nseindia.com/corporate/MARINE_24072026133342_Signed_Regulation_30_Bagging_of_Order.pdf

7. Gabriel India enters ADAS and automotive electronics through JV with Korea-based HL Klemove

Gabriel India will acquire a 30% stake in HL Klemove India for around ₹935 crore, while the Korean parent will retain the remaining 70% stake

HL Klemove India manufactures ADAS radars, front cameras, autonomous-driving control units and software, along with automotive electronics such as braking and steering ECUs

https://www.bseindia.com/xml-data/corpfiling/AttachHis/6df251ee-57b5-48ab-836c-60d324de1105.pdf

8. Sona Comstar enters into a partnership with Japanese firm Densco Corporation

Sona Comstar and DENSO will establish two India based joint ventures to develop and manufacture traction motors, inverters, generators and eAxles for electric and hybrid vehicles

The first JV will focus on high voltage liquid cooled powertrain systems for passenger and commercial vehicles, with DENSO holding 51% and Sona Comstar holding 49%. This gives Sona access to DENSO’s inverter and hybrid technology and expands it beyond individual EV components into integrated powertrain systems.

In the second JV, Sona will transfer its existing two-wheeler and three-wheeler electric motor and controller business into a subsidiary. DENSO will acquire a 49% stake at an enterprise valuation of ₹1,750 crore, while Sona retains 51% and management control.

https://www.bseindia.com/xml-data/corpfiling/AttachHis/79c5700d-fea7-4065-9651-2c9e1365c5db.pdf

9. Indo Tech Transformers enters the 400 kV transformer segment for BESS projects

Indo Tech has received NTPC approval to manufacture 400 kV class transformers for BESS projects, expanding its product portfolio beyond the existing 220 kV range
It has also secured an initial order for two 90 MVA, 400 kV transformers through an EPC contractor

Large grid scale BESS projects require high voltage transformers to connect battery systems to 220 kV and 400 kV transmission networks
NTPC’s recent renewable and BESS tenders include 400/33 kV tie transformers and 400 kV pooling substations

The approval moves Indo Tech into a more technically demanding and higher-value transformer segment and positions it to participate in NTPC’s growing BESS and renewable power evacuation pipeline

https://www.bseindia.com/xml-data/corpfiling/AttachHis/b7377360-48aa-48ed-a80b-86a90e9b668e.pdf

10. Azad Engineering delivers India’s first indigenous 350 kg thrust class expendable turbojet engine

Azad has manufactured and assembled a 350 kg thrust class turbojet engine designed by DRDO’s Gas Turbine Research Establishment, and delivered the first unit to DRDO

This is not a fighter aircraft engine, it is built for a one time use defence platform, such as a missile or unmanned system, rather than a reusable aircraft

The development is significant because Azad is moving beyond manufacturing individual aerospace components to the complete assembly of an indigenous jet engine, establishing system level manufacturing capabilities in a technology mastered by only a few countries

https://www.bseindia.com/xml-data/corpfiling/AttachHis/42c23ac8-c9c5-4e79-b588-95de5f941f31.pdf

items.title: 🚨 C2C’s auditor has issued a qualified opinion and flagged multiple serious financial and compliance concerns: 1️⃣ Liquidity & Going Concern Ris...
items.description_html:
🚨 C2C’s auditor has issued a qualified opinion and flagged multiple serious financial and compliance concerns:

1️⃣ Liquidity & Going Concern Risk:
The company is facing a liquidity crisis, with statutory dues unpaid due to lack of funds. Recovery from trade receivables remains uncertain, while operations are heavily dependent on short-term promoter funding. The auditor has raised doubt over C2C’s ability to continue as a going concern. Liquidation Risk

2️⃣ CSR Payments Not Cleared:
CSR expenses were recognised through cheques, creating a book overdraft. However, the cheques were not presented for payment. The auditor noted that the CSR obligation is discharged only when the payment is actually cleared.

3️⃣ Statutory Dues Pending:
Undisputed statutory payments remain unpaid. No provision has been made for possible interest or penalties. Delays in filing statutory returns and weak internal controls were also highlighted.

4️⃣ Labour Code Impact Not Assessed:
The company has not quantified the potential impact of new labour regulations on gratuity, provident fund, wages and other employee benefits.

5️⃣ FEMA Compliance Issues:
Overseas receivables remain unrealised beyond RBI timelines. Applications for regularisation are pending, SOFTEX registration is yet to be approved, and possible penalties have not been provided for.

items.title: We initiated Sansera for our subscribers around 16th December 2025. But the more important thing is how we filtered on this idea. > First key factor w...
items.description_html:
We initiated Sansera for our subscribers around 16th December 2025.

But the more important thing is how we filtered on this idea.

> First key factor we observed was the product mix change, where the company's intent was to gradually move from its ICE component business to Aero/Defence/Semicon (ADS) business.

> This product mix shift was visible from the fact that margins had been improving over the last 2 quarters, and growth was starting to pick up. That's how it came under our filters.

> Going a little deeper, we understood that the kind of things it was doing in the ADS business were quite moated. It had a single-source monopoly on Airbus A350/A320 thrust-reversal gimbals with zero defects over 12 years; hogging (machining from solid billet vs. forging) is a much harder-to-replicate capability for aerospace tolerances.

> Also, in its semiconductor business, it was working with Lam Research, where this year their business is expected to go from $10M to $30M .

> Also, as per our channel checks, they had orders/interest from Rolls-Royce for aero-engine feelers, the MMRFIC JV (navy fuses, radars), and a Tesla ESS order.

> All these things were a confirmation of our thesis that management has the capabilities, and that the product mix is changing for good.

> They have also given strong guidance of ₹8,000 Cr in revenue, with ADS at 20–25% of overall business and blended EBITDA margins moving above the 20% mark.

On top of this, we also visited their facility, where we got to understand the manufacturing complexity involved in the components they make for their ADS business, and their capabilities in precision engineering.

The framework was simple: through scanning, found a business where earnings were breaking out and margins were improving > went through their earnings calls and found the story of the product mix change > mapped out the value chain and tried to understand Sansera's moat in the new business they were focusing on > visited their facility to verify our thesis on the company.

Disclaimer: This is not a recommendation to buy or sell. We continue to hold it in our recommendation portfolio and may change our view at any point in time.

Saito-san, the God of motors, is how Japan is able to retain its global prominence in so many foundational industries.

My industrial pilgrimage to Japan has given me new vigor 🙏
